title: Divine Mercy Sunday
hookLine: the second Sunday of Easter, named by John Paul II in 2000

lines: A NOTEBOOK IN A POLISH CONVENT.
cards: In a convent in Poland in the 1930s, a young nun with little schooling kept a notebook. Her name was Faustina Kowalska.
She wrote that Jesus had appeared to her, robed in white, with two rays streaming from his heart, one pale and one red. She was asked to have the image painted, with a short line of trust underneath.
She died of tuberculosis in 1938, at thirty-three. Sixty-two years later, in Rome, a Polish pope declared her a saint, and gave a name to the Sunday that ends the Easter octave.

teach.b: On the thirtieth of April, 2000, John Paul II canonized Faustina and announced that, from then on, the second Sunday of Easter would be called Divine Mercy Sunday across the whole Church.
The Latin word for mercy, misericordia, joins the heart, cor, to someone's misery. The readings didn't change.

The Gospel this Sunday, in every year of the cycle, is John 20: the risen Jesus walking through locked doors, breathing on the disciples, and saying, in the Douay-Rheims, "Receive ye the Holy Ghost. Whose sins you shall forgive, they are forgiven them."
He greets frightened friends who ran away with peace, shows them his wounds, and then hands them the power to forgive.
Then Thomas, who wasn't there, gets his own visit a week later, and Jesus says: "Blessed are they that have not seen, and have believed." The feast's theme was already in the text.
Faustina's image puts it in a picture: in her diary, the two rays stand for the blood and water that flowed from his side. And the line at the bottom, in her Polish, is three words, Jezu, ufam Tobie.
In English it's the line Catholics now pray: Jesus, I trust in you. A surprise: for about twenty years, the Vatican restricted this devotion, partly because of flawed copies of her writings.

The restriction was lifted in 1978, the year a cardinal from Kraków, where she had lived, became pope. Catholics are free to take up Faustina's devotions or not; the Church approves them without requiring them.
But the line itself is short enough for anyone to carry.

teach.h: BLESSED ARE THEY THAT HAVE NOT SEEN.
teach.b: In English, five words. Not I understand. Not I'm sure.

how: On Divine Mercy Sunday Catholic parishes often display the Divine Mercy image, hear the Gospel of doubting Thomas from John 20, offer confession, and pray the Divine Mercy chaplet, often at three in the afternoon; the words Jesus, I trust in you are printed beneath the image.

games.q: the risen Jesus walks through a locked door into a room of friends who ran away from him. he greets them with peace and shows his wounds. then he breathes on them. what does he give them?
games.why: he breathes on them: receive ye the Holy Ghost; whose sins you shall forgive, they are forgiven them.

practice: Let your breathing settle and name one thing you're carrying that you can't fix today. If you pray, say Faustina's line on your breath, in on Jesus and out on the rest: Jesus, I trust in you.
If you don't pray, simply hold the worry in an open hand instead of a fist.

wordCard.voice: misericordia. The Latin word for mercy, joining heart to someone's misery, behind the feast John Paul II named in 2000, when he canonized Saint Faustina. Today's word.

orig.note: Latin: mercy — the heart (cor) given to someone's misery (miseria).

carryVoice: Your line: Jesus, I trust in you. It fits on a single breath. Until tomorrow.
